summary: Describes the Basic Mode of Layer 1 VPNs, which is port-based. The basic service is a Label Switched Path between customer ports within a VPN. It covers the operational model using provisioning or auto-discovery, and signaling extensions. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: A shared fiber network can give a customer a private link between their sites. Basic mode ties private links to specific ports.

questions: what is a port information table
subtitle: How a provider sells port-based private optical and TDM connections, with customers setting up the paths themselves using GMPLS signaling.

tldr.problem: A Layer 1 provider wants to offer customers private connections between their ports, without letting customers see the provider network and without reconfiguring provider devices each time a customer wants a path.
tldr.mechanism: Each provider edge device keeps a Port Information Table per VPN that maps customer port identifiers to provider port identifiers. Customer edge devices signal with GMPLS RSVP-TE, and the PEs swap the identifiers or build a separate PE-to-PE session.
tldr.outcome: The basic unit of service is a Label Switched Path between a pair of customer ports in a VPN. The provider limits which ports can connect, and the customers choose the actual paths.

facts.label: Basic unit of service
facts.value: An LSP between a pair of customer ports

facts.label: Port to VPN
facts.value: At most one L1VPN per PE port

today: RFC 5251 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its companion applicability statement is RFC 5253.

sections.title: The Layer 1 VPN Setting
sections.content:
RFC 5251 describes the Basic Mode of Layer 1 VPNs (L1VPN BM), outlined in RFC 4847. The service provider network is made of GMPLS-capable devices such as lambda switch capable devices, optical cross-connects and SONET/SDH cross-connects. They are split into P (provider) devices and PE (provider edge) devices. A PE connects to other devices in the network and to CE (Customer Edge) devices outside it.

The mechanisms use off-line provisioning or VPN auto-discovery, together with GMPLS signaling (RFC 3471, RFC 3473), routing (RFC 4202) and LMP (RFC 4204). Inside the provider, GMPLS is used without extensions. CE-to-PE signaling follows RFC 4208. Inter-AS and inter-provider L1VPNs are beyond the scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The big cable company has inside machines and edge machines. Customers plug into the edge machines, and the edge machines talk to the inside ones.

sections.title: What the Service Looks Like
sections.content:
Basic Mode requires GMPLS RSVP-TE for signaling, both between PEs and between CE and PE. GMPLS routing on the CE-to-PE link is outside the scope of Basic Mode. A CE-PE link is a GMPLS TE link and must be of type <X, LSC> or <Y, TDM>, where X is PSC, L2SC or TDM and Y is PSC or L2SC. For a CE-PE pair there must be at least one data-bearing channel and one control-bearing channel, or else IP reachability between the CE and PE for control information.

A port is a logical grouping of physical resources connecting a CE to a PE for one L1VPN. A port on a PE is associated with at most one L1VPN (more precisely, one Port Information Table). VPN membership is set by provisioning on provider devices, so it is enforced by the provider.

Two goals shape the design. One is single-ended provisioning: adding a port to an L1VPN needs configuration changes only on the PE that has the port. The other is that CEs can set up and tear down an LSP between existing ports without any change on provider devices. The provider restricts which ports can connect, and topologies from hub-and-spoke to full mesh of point-to-point connections are possible.
sections.plainLanguage: The company decides who is allowed to call whom. Within those rules, customers dial their own calls without asking the company each time.

sections.title: Addressing and Port Identifiers
sections.content:
The provider needs a single addressing realm spanning all PEs involved. Each customer has its own addressing realm, with freedom to use private or public addresses. Customer realms may overlap each other and the provider realm. Customers do not know or understand provider addresses.

Three port identifiers result. The Customer Port Identifier (CPI) names the CE port in the customer realm. The Provider Port Identifier (PPI) names the PE port in the provider realm. The VPN-PPI names the same PE port in the customer realm, so the provider side stays hidden. Each identifier can be an address or a tuple of port index and address, in IPv4 or IPv6. If the CPI is IPv4 the VPN-PPI MUST be IPv4, and likewise for IPv6.

CE and PE also need IP connectivity for a control channel, which could be a dedicated link, a Layer 2 VPN or a Layer 3 VPN. Its only requirement is an unambiguous way to tie a control channel to one L1VPN. The control channel addresses, CE-CC-Addr and PE-CC-Addr, MUST be unique within their L1VPN and are not shared among VPNs.
sections.plainLanguage: Each port has a customer-facing name and a company-facing name. The customer only ever sees the first one, like a nickname that hides your real address.

sections.title: Port Information Tables
sections.content:
For each L1VPN with at least one port on a PE, that PE maintains a Port Information Table (PIT). It holds <CPI, PPI> tuples for all ports in the VPN, and for local ports the tuples also include the VPN-PPI. A PE MUST maintain a PIT for each L1VPN that has locally attached member CEs, and it does not need PITs for other L1VPNs.

A PIT may be filled by provisioning or by auto-discovery. For local information a PE MAY use LMP to learn the CPI and VPN-PPI link information. The mechanisms for spreading that to other PEs are out of scope, but the information is described. A single <PPI, CPI> mapping is encoded as a one-octet PPI length, the PPI, a two-octet CPI address family identifier, a CPI length and the CPI. Each tuple MUST also be tied to one or more globally unique VPN identifiers, which can encode a VPN-ID or route target. The generic identifier encoding is 8 octets. Specific auto-discovery methods are in RFC 5195 (BGP) and RFC 5252 (OSPF).
sections.plainLanguage: Each edge machine keeps a phone book for each private network. The book says which customer name goes with which company-side name.

sections.title: Signaling and Setting Up an LSP
sections.content:
The service provider does not start LSPs; the CE does. A CE is configured with the CPIs of target ports in its L1VPN and uses a subset of GMPLS signaling to ask for an LSP. The request carries the CPI of the CE's own port and the CPI of the target. The ingress PE selects the PIT, finds the PPI for the target CPI, and the request goes on until it reaches the CE that owns the target CPI. If that CE accepts, the LSP is established. A CE need not connect to every target it knows, since that is local CE policy. If two CEs try to set up LSPs to each other at once, the CE with the lower CPI can be required to terminate the LSP the other one started.

The CE-to-PE messages use the CE-CC-Addr and PE-CC-Addr as IP source and destination addresses. There are two ways to run RSVP-TE sessions.

  • Shuffling: one end-to-end session. The ingress PE replaces CPIs in the Session and Sender Template objects with PPIs using the PIT, and the egress PE reverses this. The PEs MAY filter the signaling to hide provider topology. Shuffling MUST be performed for all RSVP-TE messages at the PE edges.
  • Stitching or nesting: the PE sets up a separate PE-to-PE session compatible with the CE session. If switching type and capacity are identical the LSPs MAY be stitched (RFC 5150). If they differ but are compatible they MAY be nested (RFC 4206). The CE does not see the PE-to-PE signaling.

If a Path message arrives without an ERO, the ingress PE MUST calculate a route and put it in an ERO before forwarding. If the message has an ERO, the PE computes a path to the egress PE and inserts it.
sections.plainLanguage: The customer asks for a line to a named friend. The edge machine looks the friend up in its phone book, swaps names for its own, and passes the call along. At the other end the names are swapped back.

sections.title: Recovery and Failure Notification
sections.content:
A CE can ask for a network-protected LSP, one protected from PE to PE, using the technique in RFC 4873. Merge nodes are identified dynamically through the LSP Segment Recovery Flags in the Protection object.

For notifications, a Notify Request object MAY be put in Path or Resv messages to give the address of a CE that should be told about an LSP failure, either upstream (via Path) or downstream (via Resv). A PE that receives one SHOULD store the Notify Node Address and SHOULD include a Notify Request in the outgoing message, and MAY change the address by local policy. Including the object requests a notification on failure but does not guarantee one will be sent.
sections.plainLanguage: A customer can ask for a backup route and can ask to be told if the line breaks. The company will try to tell them but cannot promise.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Tying a port to an L1VPN (a PIT) is a configuration operation, generally done manually by the provider during provisioning. It cannot be changed through CE-PE signaling, so signaling cannot be used to deliver L1VPN traffic to the wrong customer. Operators should secure their management and configuration process, and consider data-plane verification against accidental misconfiguration. Customers may run CE-to-CE data-plane tests, and LMP can be used for such testing.

CE-PE signaling is assumed to run over a private link or a private network whose members are trusted, so the protocol exchanges here need no extra security mechanisms. An operator that wants more may use RSVP-TE authentication and integrity functions or IPsec between PE and CE. Where one private network serves several CEs, it is RECOMMENDED that each L1VPN customer have its own, and its security mechanisms SHOULD be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Which customer a port belongs to is set by the company's own staff, not by messages from customers. So a customer cannot trick the system into connecting them to someone else's line.
